cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A crest moves along a rope, but a marked bit of rope oscillates locally.
Let's make that difference numerical.
In SI units, displacement y is zero point zero two times sine of four pi x
minus twenty pi t.
Amplitude is two centimetres, wave number is four pi per metre, and angular
frequency is twenty pi radians per second.
To follow a crest, keep its phase constant.
Four pi x minus twenty pi t stays fixed, so x increases at five metres per
second.
That is the pattern speed, along positive x.
Now watch one particle at a fixed position.
Differentiate with respect to time while keeping x unchanged.
Its transverse velocity is minus zero point four pi times cosine of the phase.
At x zero and time zero, the particle is crossing equilibrium downward at
about
one point two six metres per second.
Pause: zero displacement did not mean zero velocity.
Its acceleration is minus angular frequency squared times displacement.
At that instant acceleration is zero.
A quarter period later, the particle is at its negative extreme: velocity is
zero and acceleration is upward.
There is also a useful equation check.
Taking two time derivatives gives minus omega squared times y; taking two
position derivatives gives minus k squared times y.
Their ratio gives the ideal wave equation: the second time derivative equals
pattern speed squared times the second position derivative.
This is a linear, nondispersive wave model, not a promise for every real
medium.
Always ask which rate the problem wants before substituting numbers.
Now the pattern stands still.
A two metre string fixed at both ends has displacement zero point zero four
times sine of pi x times cosine of one hundred pi t, again in SI units.
The position factor sets each particle's amplitude.
The time factor sets its oscillation.
Nodes occur where sine of pi x is zero: at zero, one and two metres.
There are two loops, so this is the second harmonic, with wavelength two
metres
and frequency fifty hertz.
Each travelling component therefore has speed one hundred metres per second.
Notice that a stationary pattern does not mean the particles are stationary.
At x equal to one quarter metre, the local amplitude is zero point zero four
divided by the square root of two, about two point eight three centimetres.
That particle's maximum transverse speed is its local amplitude times one
hundred pi, about eight point eight nine metres per second.
Why isn't it the antinode value?
Because amplitude depends on position.
Compare particles at one quarter metre and one and one quarter metres.
Their sine factors have opposite signs, so their motions are opposite at the
same time: a phase difference of pi.
Two points inside the same loop have the same temporal phase, though their
amplitudes can differ.
At a node phase of displacement is undefined because the amplitude is zero.
Finally, the four centimetre antinode amplitude comes from two equal, opposite
travelling waves, each with amplitude two centimetres.
Do not assign the full standing wave amplitude to each component.
Those checks prevent several common JEE errors.
Let's finish with a detective problem.
A reference tuning fork is two hundred and fifty six hertz.
Another fork produces four beats per second with it.
What is the unknown frequency?
Think before choosing.
It could be two hundred and fifty two or two hundred and sixty hertz.
An absolute difference does not tell us which is higher.
Now the question states that adding a small load lowers the unknown fork's
frequency, and the beats decrease from four to three per second.
If the original frequency were two hundred and fifty two, lowering it would
move it farther from the reference and increase the beats.
That contradicts the observation.
So the original frequency was two hundred and sixty hertz; after the change it
is two hundred and fifty nine, assuming the stated small change stays on the
same side of the reference.
The direction of the change matters as much as the beat count.
Why is beat frequency the full frequency difference, not half?
Adding two equal amplitude nearby tones produces a rapid carrier multiplied by
a slowly changing cosine envelope.
That signed cosine changes sign, but loudness depends on its magnitude or its
square.
Two adjacent loud maxima occur one divided by the frequency difference seconds
apart.
For a four hertz difference, they are a quarter second apart.
With unequal amplitudes, the minimum amplitude is the absolute difference of
the two amplitudes, so quiet moments need not be silence.
This elementary beat model assumes stable nearby frequencies and comparable
amplitudes.
Our routine is simple: identify the measured quantity, preserve both initial
possibilities, then use the physical change to decide.
